name: Fallibility of Gustatory Perception
what: This subtopic explores the ways in which taste perception is prone to error or individual variation, including genetic differences in taste sensitivity (supertasters), chemical manipulation of taste receptors (miraculin), and the influence of non-taste factors such as perceptual set, colour intensity, and texture on how flavours are judged.
why: Gustatory perception is often assumed to be straightforward and reliable, but this subtopic reveals that taste is deeply shaped by biology, expectations, and other senses. Understanding these influences has practical implications for food science, marketing, and health behaviour.

items.title: I can define supertasters and describe their key biological characteristics
items.what: Supertasters are individuals who have a significantly low threshold for taste stimuli and an unusually high number of taste buds (papillae) on the tongue. They are particularly sensitive to bitter tastes and were identified by Linda Bartoshuk (1994), who found that approximately 25% of people showed extreme sensitivity to the bitter chemical PROP.
items.why: Supertasters demonstrate that biological differences between individuals lead to genuinely different taste experiences, even when tasting the same food. This is a named example in the study design.
items.example: A supertaster eating a piece of dark chocolate with 85% cocoa may find it overwhelmingly bitter and unpleasant, while a non-supertaster eating the same piece finds it pleasantly intense. The supertaster's papillae density means more taste receptor contact per bite.

items.title: I can explain why the experience of supertasters is not classified as a perceptual distortion
items.what: A perceptual distortion is an error in the interpretation of sensory stimuli. Supertasters' heightened sensitivity occurs at the level of sensation (more taste buds means more sensory receptors detecting the chemical signals), not during the brain's interpretation of those signals. Their perception is accurate relative to the sensory input they receive.
items.why: This distinction is a common exam question and requires students to understand the difference between sensation-level differences and perception-level distortions. Supertasters are not experiencing an error; they are accurately perceiving a more intense sensory signal.
items.example: If two people eat the same piece of broccoli and one tastes bitterness twice as intense as the other, that is because the supertaster has more papillae detecting more bitter compounds. They are not misinterpreting the signal; they are receiving a stronger one.

items.title: I can describe how miraculin alters taste perception and the mechanism by which it works
items.what: Miraculin is a protein extracted from the miracle berry that makes sour foods taste sweet. It binds to the taste receptors on the tongue that are responsible for detecting sweet flavours and activates them when an acidic (sour) environment is created in the mouth. It does not change the functioning of the sour taste buds themselves.
items.why: Miraculin is a named example in the study design and illustrates how the perceptual experience of taste can be deliberately manipulated through a chemical mechanism. It reinforces the idea that taste perception is not a fixed, objective reading of food.
items.example: A person who eats a miracle berry tablet and then bites into a lemon perceives the lemon as tasting sweet rather than sour. The lemon has not changed; miraculin has activated the person's sweet receptors in response to the acid in the lemon juice.

items.title: I can explain how perceptual set influences the judgement of flavours and give an example
items.what: A perceptual set is a predisposition to perceive certain features of sensory stimuli while ignoring others, shaped by expectations, past experiences, beliefs, and culture. When applied to taste, a perceptual set can cause a person to rate the flavour of food differently based on non-taste information such as branding, packaging, or prior reputation, creating a perceptual distortion.
items.why: Perceptual set is a key concept across multiple areas of the unit, and its application to taste demonstrates how psychological and social factors can override objective sensory information. It also connects to the study of top-down processing.
items.example: In a study by Bellizzi and Martin (1982), participants rated the same jelly as tasting better when it was labelled as a name brand than when labelled as a generic brand, even though the jelly was physically identical in both jars.

items.title: I can explain how colour intensity influences flavour judgement
items.what: More intensely coloured food or drink is generally perceived as having a stronger or more intense flavour, even when the actual chemical composition of the flavour is identical to a less intensely coloured version. This is because prior experience has established an expectation that brighter colour indicates greater ripeness or flavour concentration.
items.why: This phenomenon demonstrates how visual information from one sense can override or reshape the experience of another sense (taste), illustrating the interconnected and interpretive nature of perception.
items.example: Studies by Johnson and Clydesdale (1982) and Roth and colleagues (1988) found that a more deeply coloured drink was rated as tasting sweeter than a paler drink of identical sugar content, showing colour intensity acting as a false cue for sweetness.

items.title: I can describe two ways that texture influences the perception of flavour
items.what: First, texture affects the intensity of flavour by determining how much of the food contacts taste receptors and for how long. Liquid foods expose more surface area to receptors than solid forms of the same food. Second, texture affects the enjoyment of flavour through expectations about how a food should feel, which are informed by prior experience.
items.why: Understanding the two-pathway influence of texture (intensity through receptor contact, and enjoyment through expectation) allows students to give precise and complete answers about how texture operates, including identifying which of the two constitutes a perceptual distortion.
items.example: Orange juice generally tastes more intensely orange than eating an orange segment because the liquid form contacts more taste receptors per sip (intensity, not a perceptual distortion). Soft crackers taste worse than expected because they violate the expectation of crunchiness (enjoyment distortion via expectation).

items.title: I can identify which influences on flavour judgement constitute perceptual distortions and which do not
items.what: Perceptual set and colour intensity both constitute perceptual distortions because they cause the brain to misinterpret the actual sensory signal from food. The intensity aspect of texture is not a perceptual distortion because the change in flavour experienced is caused by a real difference in how much of the food contacts taste receptors. The enjoyment aspect of texture may be considered a distortion when expectations override the actual sensory experience.
items.why: Exam questions regularly ask students to evaluate whether a given phenomenon is or is not a perceptual distortion, requiring a precise understanding of where in the sensation-perception chain the change occurs.
items.example: Rating a wine as tasting better because the label says it is expensive is a perceptual distortion (expectation changes interpretation). Finding that blended fruit tastes more intensely fruity than whole fruit is not a distortion (more receptor contact is a real sensory difference).
